raw_text:
The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is a cornerstone in the prevention of sudden cardiac death (SCD). However, conventional transvenous ICD (TV-ICD) systems rely on endovascular leads, which are associated with significant short- and long-term complications, including pneumothorax, cardiac perforation, lead fracture, venous occlusion, and systemic infection [1,2]. To overcome these vulnerabilities, the entirely subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed, placing both the pulse generator and lead extrathoracically [3].

Early prospective trials, such as the S-ICD investigational device exemption (IDE) study, demonstrated successful conversion of ventricular fibrillation (VF) with acceptable safety profiles [4]. The global EFFORTLESS registry subsequently confirmed these findings in a real-world cohort [5]. Pooled analyses of these early databases reported high conversion rates for spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias [6], and subsequent midterm registry data showed stable clinical outcomes [7]. Recently, the 5-year results of the S-ICD Post-Approval Study (PAS) reinforced its long-term safety, showing high shock efficacy and low complication rates in a large, real-world population [8].

The clinical utility of S-ICDs was rigorously established by two major randomized clinical trials. The prospective, head-to-head PRAETORIAN trial randomized 849 patients to S-ICD or TV-ICD, demonstrating that the S-ICD was noninferior with respect to a composite endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [9]. Concurrently, the ATLAS trial randomized 503 younger patients or those with risk factors for lead complications, showing a 92% reduction in perioperative lead-related complications with the S-ICD compared to the TV-ICD [10]. These randomized data, supported by extensive meta-analyses, have firmly positioned the S-ICD as a standard-of-care alternative for patients without pacing requirements [11].

Implantation techniques have also evolved. While the S-ICD was initially implanted using a three-incision technique [3], a two-incision technique was developed to omit the superior parasternal incision, reducing procedural times and improving cosmetic outcomes [12]. Furthermore, adopting an intermuscular pocket (placed between the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi) instead of a subcutaneous pocket has been shown to reduce post-operative pain and generator-related complications [13].

Patient selection hinges on pre-implantation electrocardiographic (ECG) screening. Because the S-ICD senses far-field cardiac signals, patients must pass a morphological screening template to prevent T-wave oversensing (TWOS) [14]. Clinical cohorts demonstrate that while up to 90% of patients are eligible, screening failure is associated with specific ECG phenotypes such as prolonged QRS duration or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy [15]. Dynamic changes in sensing vectors during exercise or posture changes also require careful evaluation, particularly in pediatric and congenital heart disease populations where cardiac morphology changes with growth [16].

Historically, inappropriate shocks (IAS) due to cardiac oversensing (e.g., TWOS) or supraventricular tachycardias were a primary drawback of the S-ICD [17-19]. Over the past decade, technological and programming advances have mitigated this issue. High-pass filtering via the SMART Pass algorithm significantly attenuates low-frequency T-wave signals, reducing IAS by up to 68% without compromising VF detection [20]. The UNTOUCHED trial demonstrated that utilizing contemporary programming (dual-zone therapy with high-rate cutoffs) and the SMART Pass filter achieved an exceptionally low IAS rate of 3.1% at one year [21]. Secondary analyses of the PRAETORIAN trial further verified that appropriate shocks delivered by the S-ICD successfully terminate spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias [22]. Long-term follow-up of the EFFORTLESS registry [23], the application of the radiologic PRAETORIAN score to predict defibrillation success [24], and long-term cohort studies [25] have validated the overall durability and safety of the system. Notably, ATLAS trial data confirmed that these benefits are accompanied by a preserved device-specific quality of life [26]. The S-ICD is also highly valuable in patients undergoing transvenous lead extraction for systemic device infections, preventing the reintroduction of intravascular hardware [27].

Despite its success, the S-ICD has a notable limitation: it cannot provide chronic bradycardia pacing or anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) [9]. While the recently introduced extravascular ICD (EV-ICD) uses a substernal lead to deliver ATP [28], modular cardiac rhythm management (mCRM) offers an alternative solution. Early studies demonstrated the feasibility of a hybrid approach combining a leadless pacemaker (LP) with an S-ICD [29]. This concept culminated in the landmark MODULAR ATP trial, which proved that an intercommunicating, wireless mCRM system—wherein the S-ICD detects ventricular tachycardia and commands the leadless pacemaker to deliver ATP—is safe and highly effective [30].

In conclusion, the S-ICD has transitioned from a niche technology to a mainstream therapy for sudden cardiac death prevention. By avoiding intravascular complications, it offers clear advantages for a broad population of ICD candidates. Refinements in sensing algorithms and the advent of modular pacing-defibrillator systems will continue to expand the scope and safety of subcutaneous defibrillator therapy.
